newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian government, opposition prepare for OSCE.
newsitem.headline: Serbian government, opposition prepare for OSCE.

text.p: A pan-European delegation was due to visit Yugoslavia on Friday to investigate allegations of electoral fraud that have sparked a month of street protests against Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.

The delegation from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), led by former Spanish Prime Minister Filipe Gonzales, was expected to meet Milosevic and leaders of the opposition Zajedno coalition.
"We believe that all this should be resolved within the institutions of the system," Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic told a news conference on Thursday.

Milosevic invited the OSCE to send a delegation to Belgrade after 33 days of protests over alleged vote-rigging which overtuned opposition victories in 15 of Serbia's biggest towns, including the capital.
Local election commissions annulled most of Zajedno's victories in polling on November 17, citing "irregularities" -- often for obscure technical hitches.
The commissions ordered fresh elections, most of them boycotted by Zajedno, which handed control of most of the municipalities to Milosevic's Socialist Party.
Since then poll results have shunted from court to court in a complicated series of legal appeals that even Zajedno's lawyers admit they are having trouble understanding.

"All I can say is that I wish the OSCE lots of luck," said one Western diplomat. "They are going to need it if they plan to make any clear-cut statement that settles this mess after just a couple of days of talking."

Milutinovic said the government would need to consider the OSCE recommendations. "They are here to establish the facts. Naturally whatever the OSCE mission concludes, our competent institutions will have to assess within the organs of the system," he told a news conference.

Zajedno has also welcomed the OSCE mission as yet another chance for the international community to apply pressure on Milosevic, but said it would not be diverted from its mission to have the annulled results restored.

In Belgrade student leaders said they would mobilise their supporters to blockade three bridges over the Sava River to snarl up traffic going into Belgrade with the aim of paralysing the city for 30 minutes.
Zajedno hopes to repeat Thursday's protest which attracted over 200,000 people -- one of the biggest so far.

"The regime will yield, either under our pressure or from its own weaknesses," Zoran Djindjic, an opposition leader told Thursday's rally. "We are persevering in our demands; the monolith is slowly cracking."
